description: Hi! I’m a high school student from Tampa who likes building technology that solves real problems. I know JavaScript and data analysis, and I’m good at pitching and presenting. I want to build an app that turns the NASA data into something that people can actually use, like protecting outdoor workers from heat. I'm looking for determined teammates who will put in real work.
summary: Climate Detective is a website that shows which parts of a place’s climate are really changing. You can click any spot on Earth, or pick a whole country or continent. The app gets over 40 years of NASA climate data for 10 things, like temperature, rain, and wind. Then it uses math tests to check if each one is actually changing or just going up and down by chance. It ranks the results and then explains them in simpler words. This helps with the challenge’s main problem, which is that there are so many climate variables that it’s hard to know exactly which ones even matter. For countries and continents, the map shows a colored dot for each location, so you can see if something is going up in one area and down in another. details:
What it does:
Climate Detective is a website that shows which parts of a place’s climate are really changing. You can click any spot on Earth, or pick a whole country or continent. The app gets over 40 years of NASA climate data (1981 to 2025) for 10 different variables, like temperature, rain, humidity, wind, sunlight, and soil moisture. Then it checks each one to see if it is really changing, ranks them, and explains the results and gives a chart.

How it works:
First, we turn the data into one number per year, so summer and winter don’t mess up the results. Then we use two math tests that scientists use a lot. The Mann-Kendall test checks if something keeps going up or down, or if it’s just random. Sen’s slope shows how fast it is changing. We rank the results by how big the change is compared to normal ups and downs. For countries and continents, the app picks up to 16 or 30 spots, averages them, and puts a colored dot on the map for each spot. This way you can see if something is going up in one area but down in another.

How we checked it:
We tested our results for Tampa against a real NOAA weather station at Tampa International Airport and NASA satellite rain data. We found that at the weather station, nights are warming about 2.2 times faster than days. NASA’s data shows the same thing: Tampa’s coldest night of the year has warmed about 5 degrees F since 1981.

Why it matters:
There are thousands of different climate variables, and most people don’t know which ones matter depending on where they live. Climate Detective does the work for them, so students, farmers, or city planners can quickly see what is changing. We were also honest about its limits. It shows what changed, not why, and a “Possible trend” could also sometimes be a false alarm.

Tools we used:
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. MapLibre for the map, Chart.js for the charts, Natural Earth for map outlines, and GitHub Pages to host the website. You can also download the data as a spreadsheet file and share a link to any result.
projectRefs: NOAA Climate Data Online (Tampa Airport station)
